gnosh: an AI harness that thinks in Gno.

Usage
  gnosh [flags] [prompt]
      Open a session in this folder. A prompt, if there is one, is sent as its
      first message.
  gnosh -p [flags] [prompt]
      Answer one prompt and exit: print mode. Text piped in goes before the
      prompt.
  gnosh <command> [flags] [arguments]
      Run one of the commands below. "gnosh <command> --help" explains it.

Commands
  doctor                  Check that a turn could run here. (Not built yet.)
  trust [folder]          Trust a folder's own settings, list the trusted
                          folders, or forget one. (Not built yet.)
  models                  List the models each provider offers. (Not built
                          yet.)
  session <command>       Look at and manage sessions. (Not built yet.)
  mem [show|find|log]     Read the project's mem, without a model. (Not built
                          yet.)
  prompt <command>        Read gnosh's own words to the model, and make any of
                          them yours. (Not built yet.)
  agents                  The sessions that run in the background, and those
                          that ran: a view of them on a terminal. (Not built
                          yet.)
  logs [session]          Print the end of the project's log, or follow it.
                          (Not built yet.)
  attach <session>        Open the agent view on a session that runs in the
                          background. (Not built yet.)
  stop <session>          Stop a session that runs in the background. (Not
                          built yet.)
  dirs                    Say which config and data folders are in use. (Not
                          built yet.)
  ssh [ssh args]          Run ssh, putting what the far side copies on this
                          machine's clipboard. (Not built yet.)
  mcp <command>           Add, list, show and remove MCP servers. (Not built
                          yet.)
  help [command]          Show gnosh's help, or a command's.
  version                 Print which build of gnosh this is.

Which conversation
  -c, -C, --continue
      Continue the most recent session of this project. (-c used to take the
      working folder, which is --cwd now. So a single word right after -c is
      refused: write -C before a one-word prompt.)
  -r, --resume [session]
      Resume a session by its ID or its name, or by words in its name or first
      prompt when one session alone has them, or from a transcript file given
      as an absolute path ending in .jsonl. With nothing after it, show the
      sessions to pick from; in print mode a session must be named. The
      argument after -r is always taken as the session, never as the prompt.
  --session-id <uuid>
      Give the new conversation this ID, which must be a UUID. It is for a new
      conversation only: not with -c, -r or --fork-session.
  --fork-session
      With -c or -r: go on in a copy of the session and leave the original as
      it was. (Not built yet.)
  -n, --name <name>
      Name the session: the new one, the one resumed, or the --fork-session
      copy. (Not built yet.)
  --bg, --background
      Start the session in the background and return at once: it works on the
      prompt as a run of its own, as /background has a session go on, and
      gnosh says its ID and how to follow it (gnosh agents, gnosh logs, gnosh
      stop, gnosh -r). A call that needs a yes waits for one in gnosh agents,
      listed there under Needs input. With -c, or -r and a session's ID or
      name, it goes on with that session instead of a new one. Not with -p,
      --fork-session or --no-session-persistence. (Not built yet.)

Which model
  -m, --model <model>
      Use this model for this run only, written as model or provider/model.
      Nothing is saved.
  --reasoning-effort, --effort <level>
      How hard the model thinks in this run. The levels depend on the model.
      (Not built yet.)
  --fallback-model <models>
      Models to go on with, tried in order, when the model cannot answer (its
      server is down, not ready or too busy): up to three, separated by
      commas. The switch holds for the rest of the turn; the next one asks the
      model first again. (Not built yet.)

Permissions
  -y, --yolo, --dangerously-skip-permissions
      Skip every permission question; the same as --permission-mode
      bypassPermissions. A print run refuses whatever would have asked, unless
      it is given this, a permission mode or allow rules.
  --permission-mode <mode>
      Start in this permission mode: default (also written manual), plan,
      acceptEdits, dontAsk or bypassPermissions. (Not built yet.)
  --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions
      Let the session switch to skipping permissions later, with Shift+Tab,
      without starting that way. (Not built yet.)
  --allowedTools, --allowed-tools <rules...>
      Let these run without asking. A rule is a tool's name, or a name with a
      pattern in parentheses: Read, "Bash(git diff *)". (Not built yet.)
  --disallowedTools, --disallowed-tools <rules...>
      Refuse these. A bare tool name takes the tool away from the model; a
      rule with a pattern refuses only the calls it matches. (Not built yet.)
  --tools <names...>
      Give the model only these built-in tools. "" gives it none, and default
      gives it all of them. (Not built yet.)
  --add-dir <dirs...>
      Let the agent read files in these other folders without asking. Each
      must exist. (Not built yet.)
  --trust-folder
      Use this folder's own settings for this one run, without recording the
      folder as trusted. (Not built yet.)

What the model is told
  --system-prompt <text>
      Use this text in place of gnosh's own instructions. (Not built yet.)
  --system-prompt-file <path>
      The same, with the text read from a file. Given together with
      --system-prompt, the file's text comes first. (Not built yet.)
  --append-system-prompt <text>
      Add this text to the end of the instructions. (Not built yet.)
  --append-system-prompt-file <path>
      The same, with the text read from a file. Given together with
      --append-system-prompt, the file's text comes first. (Not built yet.)
  --agents <json>
      Kinds of sub-agent for this run, over those of the files and gnosh's
      own: a JSON object of agents by name, each with "description" and
      "prompt" and the settings of an agent file ("tools", "model", "maxTurns"
      ...), or the path of a file that holds one. (Not built yet.)
  --agent <name>
      Run the session as this kind of agent: its prompt in place of gnosh's
      own, its tools, and its model. It outranks the setting "agent"; a
      session that ran as an agent runs as it again when it is resumed. (Not
      built yet.)

Settings for this run
  --cwd <dir>
      Work in this folder instead of the current one.
  --worktree [name]
      Work in a git work tree of the repository's own, in
      .gnosh/worktrees/<name> on the branch worktree-<name>, made at the
      commit checked out; one of that name already there is opened again.
      Without a name, one is made up. A work tree left as it was made is
      removed when the session ends, unless it was named; any other is kept.
      The folder must be trusted. (Not built yet.)
  --settings <file-or-json>
      Extra settings for this run: a file, or the JSON itself. They win over
      the settings files for the keys they name.
  --setting-sources <list>
      Which settings files to read: any of user, project and local, with
      commas between. (Not built yet.)
  --mcp-config <files-or-json...>
      MCP servers for this run, as files or the JSON itself, each in the shape
      of .mcp.json. A run waits for them before its turn. (Not built yet.)
  --strict-mcp-config
      Use only the MCP servers --mcp-config gives. (Not built yet.)
  --channels <servers...>
      MCP servers whose events come into this session as they happen, each as
      server:<name>: a stdio server of your MCP configuration that declares
      itself a channel, as Claude Code's do (a CI webhook, a chat bridge). The
      model sees each event and may answer through the server's own tools.
      (Not built yet.)
  --dangerously-load-development-channels <servers...>
      The same as --channels, which gnosh keeps no list of approved channels
      for: Claude Code's spelling for a channel of one's own. (Not built yet.)
  --safe-mode
      Start with your customizations off (hooks, MCP servers, context files,
      skills on disk, custom commands), to fix a broken one. Providers, the
      model, built-in tools and permissions stay as they are. (Not built yet.)
  --bare
      Minimal mode: no hooks, skills, custom commands, MCP servers from files,
      context files or mem; only Bash, Read, Edit and Write (unless --tools
      says otherwise); no background commands or sub-agents. Give the run what
      it needs with flags: --append-system-prompt, --settings, --mcp-config,
      --add-dir. (Not built yet.)
  --disable-slash-commands
      Turn off skills and slash commands for this session. (Not built yet.)
  -d, --debug[=filter]
      Write more to the log. A filter keeps only some kinds, and must be
      attached with an equals sign: --debug=hooks,mcp. (Not built yet.)
  --debug-file <path>
      Write the debug log to this file. Turns --debug on. (Not built yet.)
  --verbose
      Show each turn in full. In print mode: the log, and one line per
      finished tool call, on stderr. With -p, -v means this. (Not built yet.)

Print mode
  -p, --print
      Answer one prompt and exit, without the interface. Every word after it
      that is not a flag is the prompt.
  --output-format <format>
      What to print: text (the answer, and the default), json (one result
      object at the end) or stream-json (a JSON line per message, then the
      result). (Not built yet: json, stream-json.)
  --input-format <format>
      What standard input carries: text (the prompt, and the default), or
      stream-json (one JSON user message a line, for a conversation that goes
      on until standard input closes; needs --output-format stream-json). (Not
      built yet: stream-json.)
  --goal <condition>
      Keep working until this condition holds, as /goal does in a session. The
      run exits non-zero while the goal is still unmet. (Not built yet.)
  --max-turns <n>
      Stop after this many turns of the model. There is no limit unless this
      is given.
  --small-model <model>
      The model for the run's short side jobs. Without it they use the main
      model. (Not built yet.)
  --include-partial-messages
      With --output-format stream-json: also write the replies as they arrive,
      as the Messages API's streaming events (stream_event lines). (Not built
      yet.)
  --replay-user-messages
      With --input-format and --output-format stream-json: write each user
      message read back on standard output, as a user line with isReplay. (Not
      built yet.)
  --json-schema <schema>
      After the turn, have the result as JSON that conforms to this JSON
      Schema: in the result's structured_output with --output-format json, and
      alone on standard output with text. (Not built yet.)
  --permission-prompts <who>
      Who answers a call that needs a person's yes: host (the default; a run
      has no host to ask, so the call is refused) or none (refused, the model
      is told not to send it again, and the tools that ask a person are taken
      away). (Not built yet.)
  --no-session-persistence
      Keep nothing of the run: its session is not saved, and cannot be
      resumed. (Not built yet.)

Help and version
  -h, --help
      Show help: gnosh's, or after a command's name that command's.
  -v, --version
      Print which build of gnosh this is: when it was built, and from which
      commit. (With -p, -v means --verbose.)

Reading the command line
  Flags go before or after the prompt, in any order. Everything after a lone
  -- is the prompt, even if it begins with a dash.

  A list flag (--allowedTools, --disallowedTools, --tools, --add-dir,
  --mcp-config, --channels, --dangerously-load-development-channels) takes the
  argument after it, and then each argument after that up to the next flag,
  for as long as the argument has no space in it (spaces inside parentheses do
  not count). So a prompt of two words or more ends a list (gnosh stops to ask
  if that prompt reads like more tools), but a one-word prompt right after a
  list would join it: put the prompt first, put -- before it, or attach the
  list with an equals sign, as in --tools=Read,Edit.

  In a list of tools or rules, commas and spaces separate the items, but not
  inside parentheses: "Bash(git diff *),Edit" is two rules.

  A value that begins with a dash is attached with an equals sign:
  --name=-draft. A flag typed twice counts the last time, except list flags,
  which add up. One-letter flags can share a dash (-yC); one that takes a
  value goes last, and its value is the next argument.

  A first word that is one of the commands above is that command, not a
  prompt. To send such a word as a prompt, put -- before it, or use -p.
